What Is Elevation Cladding

Elevation cladding refers to any material applied as an outer layer over a building's structural wall, primarily to protect it from weather and to define its visual appearance. Unlike plaster and paint, which are applied directly and bond to the wall surface, cladding is typically installed on a substructure, a frame of metal or timber battens fixed to the wall, which creates an air gap behind the finished surface. That gap matters more than most homeowners realise, since it allows drainage, ventilation and thermal separation between the outer material and the wall behind it, which is part of why well-installed cladding systems often outperform direct-applied finishes over the long term, particularly in India's combination of intense sun and heavy monsoon rainfall.
Types of Elevation Cladding Materials

Metal cladding: aluminium, steel or Corten panels in flat, fluted, perforated or parametric formats, offering the widest design range and, when properly coated, the longest service life among common cladding materials. Fibre cement panels: a lightweight, flat panel option used for its balance of cost and clean finish, though performance varies significantly by grade and manufacturer. Stone veneer: thin-cut natural or engineered stone, used for a premium, textured appearance, particularly effective at plinth level or as an accent. Brick cladding and brick-look tile: a durable, low-maintenance option that adds warmth and texture, popular for both full facades and accent strips. Wood and WPC (wood-plastic composite) panels: used for warmth and a natural look, with WPC offering better weather resistance than genuine timber in Indian conditions. Glass and structural glazing: used selectively for light and a contemporary look, typically combined with a solid cladding material rather than covering an entire facade. Texture paint and plaster finishes: technically a direct-applied finish rather than true cladding, but included here as the baseline comparison most homeowners weigh cladding options against.
Elevation Cladding Materials Compared by Cost, Lifespan and Maintenance

Texture paint and plaster remain the least expensive option, typically ₹150 to ₹300 per square foot, but require repainting every four to six years and offer the shortest effective lifespan before visible wear appears. Brick and tile cladding generally runs ₹300 to ₹600 per square foot, is extremely low maintenance, and can last several decades with only occasional cleaning. Stone veneer typically costs ₹350 to ₹900 per square foot depending on stone type, is highly durable, but is heavier and needs correct structural support for larger applications. Fibre cement panels range roughly ₹250 to ₹500 per square foot for standard grades, need minimal maintenance for the first several years but can show fading or warping earlier than metal systems if a lower grade board was used. Engineered metal cladding systems, including aluminium and steel panels with proper coating, generally cost ₹800 to ₹2,500 per square foot installed, and are the category most likely to carry a formal 15 to 30 year coating warranty, making the higher upfront cost easier to justify against total cost of ownership over two to three decades.
Best Elevation Cladding Materials by Climate Zone

In coastal regions, including Mumbai, Chennai, Kochi and Goa, salt-laden air accelerates corrosion on lower grade metals and can degrade certain stone types over time, making marine-grade aluminium with a robust PVDF coating and careful joint detailing the safer long-term choice over untreated steel or porous stone. In hot, dry climates such as Rajasthan, much of Gujarat and inland NCR, intense UV exposure is the primary threat, and heat-reflective coatings along with materials that do not absorb and re-radiate heat, such as lighter coloured metal panels or well-insulated cladding systems, perform noticeably better than dark, heat-absorbing finishes on west and south-facing walls. In high-rainfall regions across the Northeast, Western Ghats and coastal Karnataka and Kerala, drainage detailing behind the cladding matters more than the surface material itself, since even a premium finish will fail prematurely if water is allowed to pool or seep behind the panel during extended monsoon periods.
Metal Elevation Cladding: Why It Is Gaining Ground in India

Metal cladding has moved from a niche architectural choice to a mainstream option across Indian residential and commercial projects over the past several years, driven largely by its combination of design flexibility and genuinely long service life when specified correctly. Unlike stone or brick, metal panels can be formed into fluted, perforated, folded or fully parametric patterns, giving architects and homeowners far more creative range without sacrificing durability. Unlike lighter composite boards or texture paint, a properly coated metal system does not need to be repainted or replaced within a five to ten year window, which changes the total cost calculation significantly once maintenance and replacement cycles are factored in rather than comparing only the initial installed price. How to Choose the Right Elevation Cladding Material

Identify the climate zone the building sits in and shortlist only materials proven to perform in that specific combination of heat, humidity and rainfall. Set a total budget for the cladding area specifically, separate from the overall construction budget, so material comparisons are made on realistic numbers. Decide whether cladding will cover the full facade or be used selectively as an accent, since this materially changes which materials remain affordable. Ask for the coating or treatment specification in writing, not just the base material name, since two panels of the same metal can perform very differently depending on finish grade. Confirm substructure and drainage detailing before installation begins, since this is the single biggest factor in how long any cladding system actually lasts.
Installation and Maintenance Basics

Most elevation cladding systems are installed on a substructure of metal or timber battens fixed to the structural wall, with the cladding panels then mounted onto that frame using clips, screws or a concealed fixing system depending on the material. This substructure is what creates the drainage air gap behind the panels and is also what allows individual panels to be removed and replaced if damaged, without disturbing the surrounding cladding, which is one of the practical advantages cladding systems have over direct-applied finishes like plaster. Maintenance requirements vary by material but are generally light for well-specified systems: metal and stone cladding typically need only an annual wash to remove dust and pollution buildup, while fibre cement and other lower grade boards may need more frequent inspection for early signs of fading or edge lifting.
Common Cladding Mistakes to Avoid

Choosing a cladding material based only on the sample shown in a showroom without checking how it performs outdoors in the specific city's climate. Skipping or under-specifying the drainage gap behind the cladding to save on substructure cost, which is the most common cause of early failure. Mixing too many cladding materials across one facade, which increases both cost and the number of junctions that need careful waterproofing detailing. Assuming all panels of the same material are equivalent regardless of coating grade or manufacturer, when performance can vary significantly between suppliers. Finalising cladding choice after the building shell is already complete, rather than planning substructure fixing points during the structural design stage.
Sustainability and Energy Performance of Cladding Materials

Elevation cladding is not just a visual decision, it also affects how much heat a building absorbs and how much energy is spent cooling it, which matters across most of India for a large part of the year. Ventilated cladding systems, where an air gap sits between the cladding and the structural wall, naturally reduce heat transfer compared with a direct-applied finish, since the trapped air layer acts as a buffer rather than allowing heat to conduct straight through to the interior. Lighter coloured and reflective metal finishes further reduce solar heat gain compared with dark, heat-absorbing surfaces, which is particularly relevant on west-facing walls that receive the most intense afternoon sun in Indian cities. Material lifespan is itself a sustainability factor that is easy to overlook. A cladding system rated for 25 to 30 years, replaced once every three decades, has a meaningfully smaller lifecycle footprint than a plaster finish that needs full repainting, including surface preparation and paint production, every four to six years across the same period. This is one of the arguments increasingly used by architects specifying metal cladding on projects where long-term building performance, not just initial appearance, is part of the brief.
Cladding for Renovation Projects vs New Builds

Adding cladding to an existing building during a renovation involves a different set of considerations than specifying it for a new build. On an existing structure, the condition of the underlying wall, including any dampness, cracks or previous waterproofing failures, needs to be assessed and corrected before a substructure is fixed to it, since cladding installed over an unresolved underlying issue will only mask the problem temporarily rather than solve it. Renovation projects also need to account for existing window and door positions, drainage pipes, and electrical fittings, which a new build can plan around from the start but a renovation must work with as fixed constraints. On the positive side, renovation cladding projects are often faster to execute than the equivalent new build application, since there is no need to wait for the structural shell to be completed, and many homeowners use a cladding renovation specifically to modernise an older home's street presence without touching the interior layout at all.

Frequently Asked Questions

1. What is the difference between cladding and plaster finishing?

Plaster and paint are applied directly and bond to the wall surface, while cladding is installed on a substructure — a frame of metal or timber battens fixed to the wall — which creates an air gap behind the finished surface. That gap allows drainage, ventilation and thermal separation, which is part of why well-installed cladding systems often outperform direct-applied finishes over the long term, particularly under India's combination of intense sun and heavy monsoon rainfall.

2. Which elevation cladding material lasts the longest?

Engineered metal cladding systems, including aluminium and steel panels with a proper PVDF or comparable coating, generally carry the longest formal warranties, typically 15 to 30 years, and are the category most likely to justify their higher upfront cost against total cost of ownership over two to three decades. Brick and stone cladding are also very durable and low maintenance, though they do not carry the same kind of coating warranty.

3. How does climate affect which cladding material I should choose?

In coastal regions, salt-laden air accelerates corrosion, making marine-grade aluminium with a robust PVDF coating the safer long-term choice. In hot, dry climates, heat-reflective coatings and lighter coloured metal panels perform better than dark, heat-absorbing finishes. In high-rainfall regions, the drainage detailing behind the cladding matters more than the surface material itself, since even a premium finish will fail prematurely if water pools or seeps behind the panel.

4. What is the most common mistake when installing elevation cladding?

Skipping or under-specifying the drainage gap behind the cladding to save on substructure cost is the most common cause of early failure. Other frequent mistakes include choosing a material based only on an indoor showroom sample without checking outdoor climate performance, and mixing too many cladding materials across one facade, which increases both cost and the number of junctions that need careful waterproofing.
